newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. weather chief urges better monitoring.
newsitem.headline: U.N. weather chief urges better monitoring.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s weather agency said on Thursday the world community was wrong to rely on short-term food aid while refusing to spend money to help poor countries plan for droughts and natural disasters.

"I believe international action in the past has been focused on short-term food aid in relation to drought or conflict areas," said Godwin Obasi, secretary general of the World Meteorological Organisation.

"Let us strengthen our monitoring capabilities to improve climatological stations, then you are basing all your action and your plans on scientific information," he told a news conference at the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit.
Obasi, a Nigerian, said longer-term, systematic monitoring of climate conditions would enhance food security by ensuring that "every dollar we spend really does get the maximum benefit".

He called for investment in a network of meteorological monitoring stations that would help boost yields by providing more detailed information on when to sow and irrigate crops and may predict crises such as drought.
"If you want to manage your limited water resources, there is no other way," he said.
"The world community, I think, is not serious in abating hunger," Obasi told Reuters later.
He said farmers had already reaped rewards by switching to methods of cultivation based on climatic information. Farmers in Mali and Burkino Faso had boosted yields by up to 30 percent.
In Guatemala, he said that by sowing earlier and irrigating crops according to scientific data, farmers were able to grow two crops a year instead of one.
Asked how much money was needed to set up such a network of monitoring stations and how long it would take, Obasi said:
"Half a billion dollars and even if it was over 10 years, it would still be an improvement."

Obasi said the sea-level was forecast to rise between 15-95 cm (6.0-38 inches) over the next century and the earth's temperature could rise by 1.0 to 3.5 degrees Celsius, affecting water supply and food production in some regions.

He said the international community was making a false economy by not investing in preventive measures, citing reluctance to come up with the $25-$40 million needed to set up weather monitoring centres in Nairobi and Harare.
"Yet when drought came, they (the international community) were keen to pledge $100-$150 million (in food aid)," he said.
"Let us have a 10-15 year plan to help the vulnerable communities...respond when calamities strike them," Obasi said.
"I don't want my own grandchildren always to look for food aid."
